questions.question: You are first on scene at a multi-vehicle pile-up with ~20 patients. Your FIRST action is to:
options: B. Establish command and send a METHANE report
C. Treat the most critical patient
D. Start transporting the walking wounded
questions.rationale: Command and communication come before treatment. The first crew sets up the incident.

questions.question: In METHANE, 'E' (the first one) stands for:
questions.rationale: M-E-T-H-A-N-E: the first E is Exact location; the last E is Emergency services present/required.

questions.question: Which element of METHANE tells incoming units the safest approach route and rendezvous point?
CSCATTT places TRIAGE after:
questions.rationale: Command, Safety, Communication, Assessment, then Triage, Treatment, Transport.

questions.question: The best way to report casualty numbers early in an incident is:
options: A. Wait until all are counted
C. Leave it to the hospital
D. Give an estimate with severity breakdown
questions.rationale: Early estimates let resources move. Refine numbers in later updates.

questions.question: You arrive and see 6 office workers collapsed in a lobby, no trauma, two seizing. You should:
options: A. Start triage at the door
B. Withdraw, isolate upwind, report a suspected chemical incident and request HazMat
C. Run in and open airways
questions.rationale: Multiple collapsed people without trauma = chemical until proven otherwise. Entering makes you casualty #7.

questions.question: Why are 10-codes discouraged in MCI radio traffic?
options: D. They differ between agencies and cause confusion
questions.rationale: NIMS requires plain language to ensure interoperability across agencies.

questions.question: In the first-due crew, the member NOT in command should:
options: A. Perform a rapid recon and global sort, feeding numbers to command
B. Start IVs on red patients
questions.rationale: Recon and global triage give command the 'N' for METHANE.

questions.question: Which METHANE element is MOST often forgotten and endangers incoming crews?
questions.rationale: Omitting hazards sends crews into fire, chemicals, traffic, or violence.

questions.question: A good follow-up update structure after METHANE is:
questions.rationale: CAN updates keep command and dispatch synchronized.
